questions.question: A model reaches 99% accuracy on training data but 70% on validation data. What is the most likely problem?
options: A learning rate that is too small
Overfitting
Underfitting
Data drift
questions.explanation: A large gap between training and validation performance means the model memorized training-specific patterns and doesn't generalize, which is overfitting. Underfitting would show poor performance on both sets.

source.title: Google ML Crash Course, Overfitting

questions.question: A neural network overfits a small dataset. Which two techniques are standard ways to reduce overfitting? (Select two.)
options: Training for many more epochs
Dropout
Increasing model size substantially
Removing the validation set
Data augmentation
questions.explanation: Dropout randomly drops units during training, which prevents co-adaptation. Data augmentation creates more varied training examples. Training longer or using a bigger model usually makes overfitting worse, and removing validation only hides it.

source.title: Srivastava et al., Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting

questions.question: Which two statements about k-fold cross-validation are correct? (Select two.)
options: It trains k models and deploys all of them together as an ensemble
It makes the training set k times larger by duplicating examples
It tunes the learning rate automatically during a single training run
Every example is used for validation exactly once across the k folds
It gives a more reliable estimate than a single split, especially on small data
questions.explanation: The data is split into k folds. Each fold serves once as the validation set while the others train the model, and the k scores are averaged. All data gets used for both training and validation, which gives a steadier estimate than one split.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Cross-validation

questions.question: A team computes normalization statistics (mean and std) on the whole dataset before splitting into train and test. What is the problem?
options: Data leakage: test information influences training
The model will underfit the training data
The training set becomes smaller after scaling
Normalization never helps neural networks learn
questions.explanation: Fitting preprocessing on all data leaks information from the test set into training. Preprocessing should be fit on the training data only, for example inside a scikit-learn Pipeline, and then applied to validation and test data.

source.title: scikit-learn, Common pitfalls: Data leakage

questions.question: Which of these is an example of feature engineering?
options: Deriving 'day of week' and 'hour' from a timestamp
Choosing how many GPUs and nodes to use for training
Raising the temperature at inference time
Deploying the trained model as a REST API
questions.explanation: Feature engineering creates or transforms input variables, such as extracting date parts, encoding categories or scaling numbers, so a model can learn patterns more easily. The other options are infrastructure or inference settings.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Preprocessing data

questions.question: Which two tasks are examples of unsupervised learning? (Select two.)
options: Training a game-playing agent from rewards for winning moves
Classifying emails as spam using thousands of labeled examples
Grouping customer reviews into topics without any labels
Reducing embedding dimensions with PCA to visualize them
Predicting house prices from a table of labeled past sales
questions.explanation: Unsupervised learning finds structure, such as clusters or principal components, in unlabeled data. Predicting prices or spam from labeled examples is supervised learning, and learning from rewards is reinforcement learning.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Clustering

questions.question: What does backpropagation compute?
options: The model's predictions and accuracy on the held-out test set
The number of layers the network should have
The gradient of the loss for every weight, via the chain rule
The optimal learning rate for each training step
questions.explanation: Backpropagation applies the chain rule backwards through the network to get the gradient of the loss with respect to each parameter. An optimizer such as SGD or Adam then uses those gradients to update the weights.

source.title: NVIDIA DLI, Getting Started with Deep Learning (open materials)

questions.question: Training loss jumps around wildly and then becomes NaN in the first few hundred steps. What is the most likely first thing to check?
options: The training data is shuffled
The learning rate is too high
The model has too few output classes
The validation set is too large
questions.explanation: A learning rate that is too large makes updates overshoot, so the loss oscillates or diverges to NaN. Lowering it, adding warmup or using gradient clipping are standard fixes.

source.title: Google ML Crash Course, Linear regression: Hyperparameters

questions.question: Why are non-linear activation functions (e.g. ReLU) needed in a neural network?
options: They convert the input text into tokens
They reduce the number of parameters that each layer needs
Without them, stacked layers collapse into one linear map
They make training results fully deterministic
questions.explanation: A composition of linear layers is still linear, so the network could only learn linear functions. Non-linear activations let deep networks approximate complex functions.

source.title: Dive into Deep Learning, Multilayer Perceptrons

questions.question: For a multi-class classifier with mutually exclusive classes, which output layer and loss are standard?
options: Softmax with categorical cross-entropy
Sigmoid with mean squared error
ReLU with hinge loss
Linear output with mean absolute error
questions.explanation: Softmax turns logits into a probability distribution over classes, and cross-entropy measures the difference from the true label. Sigmoid per output is used for multi-label problems, and MSE for regression.

source.title: Keras API, Losses (CategoricalCrossentropy)

questions.question: What is the vanishing gradient problem?
options: The model forgets its training data after it is deployed
Gradients grow too large and quickly turn the loss into NaN values
The GPU runs out of memory during the backward pass
Gradients shrink through many layers, so early layers learn slowly
questions.explanation: Repeated multiplication by small derivatives, such as saturated sigmoids, makes gradients exponentially small in deep or recurrent networks. LSTMs, ReLU, residual connections and normalization were introduced partly to fix this. Exploding gradients are the opposite problem.

source.title: Dive into Deep Learning, Numerical Stability and Initialization

questions.question: A team has only 2,000 labeled medical images. What is usually the most effective approach?
options: Fine-tune a model pre-trained on a large dataset
Wait until a million labeled images are collected
Fit a linear regression on the raw pixel values
Train a very deep network from random weights
questions.explanation: Transfer learning reuses features learned on large datasets and adapts them with a small labeled set, typically by fine-tuning the top layers. It needs far less data and compute than training from scratch.

source.title: NVIDIA DLI, Getting Started with Deep Learning (open materials)

questions.question: Convolutional neural networks are particularly suited to images because:
options: Shared local filters detect the same pattern anywhere
They process every pixel independently of its neighbours
They model time order with recurrent connections
They need no labeled training data to classify images
questions.explanation: Convolutions slide small learned filters over the image. Weight sharing reduces parameters and detects the same pattern anywhere in the image, building from edges up to complex shapes.

source.title: NVIDIA DLI, Getting Started with Deep Learning (open materials)

questions.question: Which two statements about the Adam optimizer are correct? (Select two.)
options: It keeps running estimates of the first and second moments of the gradients
It adapts the effective step size for each parameter
It can only be used for linear models with a convex loss function
It needs no learning rate, because it finds the right step size by line search
It computes gradients without needing backpropagation through the network
questions.explanation: Adam combines momentum (the first-moment estimate) with RMSProp-like scaling (the second-moment estimate), which gives per-parameter adaptive step sizes. It still needs gradients from backpropagation and a base learning rate.

source.title: Kingma & Ba, Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization

questions.question: What is the role of the batch size during training?
options: The number of layers in the network
The number of times the whole dataset is seen during training
The number of output classes of the model
The number of examples used for each gradient update
questions.explanation: Batch size is how many samples are processed before each weight update. An epoch is one full pass over the dataset. Larger batches use more memory and give smoother gradient estimates.

source.title: Google ML Crash Course, Linear regression: Hyperparameters

questions.question: What does TF-IDF give a high weight to?
options: Terms that appear in every single document of the corpus
Terms frequent in a document but rare across the corpus
Words that appear in the document title only
The longest words in each document
questions.explanation: TF-IDF multiplies term frequency by inverse document frequency, so words common in one document but rare elsewhere get high weights. Words like 'the' appear everywhere and get low weights.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Text feature extraction (Tf-idf)

questions.question: What is the difference between stemming and lemmatization?
options: Stemming keeps full words; lemmatization truncates them to prefixes
Stemming uses neural networks; lemmatization uses regular expressions
Stemming strips affixes by rules; lemmatization returns dictionary forms
Lemmatization is the same as stemming but only works for numbers
questions.explanation: Stemming, such as the Porter stemmer, strips suffixes heuristically and may produce non-words ('studies' → 'studi'). Lemmatization uses vocabulary and part of speech to return the lemma ('studies' → 'study', 'better' → 'good').

source.title: spaCy, Linguistic Features: Lemmatization

questions.question: A team needs to extract company names, people and dates from contracts using a fast, production-ready Python library. Which is the most direct fit?
options: spaCy's named entity recognizer
NumPy's linear algebra module
Matplotlib
cuGraph
questions.explanation: spaCy provides pretrained pipelines with tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing and named entity recognition (ORG, PERSON, DATE...). Matplotlib is for plots, NumPy for arrays and cuGraph for graph analytics.

source.title: spaCy, Linguistic Features: Named Entities

questions.question: Part-of-speech tagging assigns each token:
options: A grammatical category such as noun or verb
A translation of the token into English text
A sentiment score between -1 and 1
A dense vector embedding of the token
questions.explanation: POS tagging labels each token with its grammatical role. It is a classic NLP pipeline step used for lemmatization, parsing and information extraction.

source.title: spaCy, Linguistic Features: Part-of-speech tagging

questions.question: Which library is primarily used for fast numerical operations on n-dimensional arrays in Python?
options: NumPy
spaCy
Matplotlib
LangChain
questions.explanation: NumPy provides the ndarray and vectorized math operations that most of the Python data and ML ecosystem builds on. spaCy is NLP, Matplotlib plotting and LangChain LLM orchestration.

source.title: Python Data Science Handbook, Introduction to NumPy

questions.question: Keras is best described as:
options: A high-level API for building and training deep learning models
A tokenizer library for subword vocabularies
A GPU driver for running CUDA kernels
A vector database for storing and searching sentence embeddings
questions.explanation: Keras is a high-level deep learning API with layers, models, losses and optimizers. Keras 3 can run on TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch backends.

source.title: Keras documentation

questions.question: How does a diffusion model generate an image?
options: It retrieves the most similar image from a database
It predicts the next pixel from left to right only
It starts from noise and denoises it step by step
It compresses an existing photo with JPEG
questions.explanation: Diffusion models are trained to reverse a gradual noising process. Generation starts from pure noise and runs the denoiser many times, removing a little noise each step until a clean sample appears.

source.title: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Demystifying Diffusion-Based Models

questions.question: During training of a diffusion model, what is the 'forward process'?
options: Turning images into text captions
Generating images from text prompts
Removing noise from images step by step
Gradually adding noise to training images
questions.explanation: The forward process is fixed: it progressively adds Gaussian noise until the data becomes pure noise. The network learns the reverse (denoising) process, which is what is used to generate.

source.title: Ho et al., Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models

questions.question: CLIP learns a shared space for images and text by:
options: Generating a caption for each training image with a diffusion model
Supervised training only on labeled ImageNet classes
Converting the text in images into strings with OCR
Contrastive training that pulls matching image-caption pairs together
questions.explanation: CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder with a contrastive objective on hundreds of millions of image-text pairs. Matching pairs end up close in a shared embedding space, which enables zero-shot classification and cross-modal search.

source.title: Radford et al., Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP)

questions.question: Which two tasks need a model that accepts non-text input, rather than a text-only LLM? (Select two.)
options: Translating a text paragraph from English to Portuguese
Classifying the sentiment of a tweet
Transcribing a recorded customer call into text
Summarizing a long text email
Answering questions about a photo of a damaged car
questions.explanation: Visual question answering needs an image input, and speech-to-text needs audio, so both need models with non-text modalities. The other three are text-in, text-out tasks.

source.title: NVIDIA Glossary, What is Generative AI?

questions.question: During pre-training, a GPT-style LLM learns mainly by:
options: Memorizing a fixed list of question-answer pairs
Playing games against itself for rewards
Predicting the next token on unlabeled text
Learning from human-labeled sentiment scores
questions.explanation: Pre-training uses self-supervision: the next token in raw text is the label, so no manual labeling is needed. Instruction tuning and RLHF come later to make the model follow instructions.

source.title: Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3)

questions.question: GPT-3 showed that large language models can perform new tasks from a few examples in the prompt. This ability is called:
options: Catastrophic forgetting
Knowledge distillation
Gradient boosting
In-context learning
questions.explanation: In-context learning means the model adapts its behaviour from instructions and demonstrations in the prompt without weight updates. GPT-3 showed it improves with model scale.

source.title: Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3)

questions.question: You must choose between a gradient-boosted tree model and a small neural network for a tabular dataset of 50,000 rows. Which two practices make the comparison fair? (Select two.)
options: Evaluate both on the same held-out data or the same cross-validation folds
Use a different random train/test split for each of the two models
Report training accuracy as the main result for both models
Use the same evaluation metric that matches the business goal
Tune only the neural network, because tree models need no tuning
questions.explanation: A fair model comparison uses identical data splits and the same relevant metric, ideally with comparable tuning effort for each model. Training accuracy and different splits make the comparison unreliable.

source.title: scikit-learn User Guide, Cross-validation

questions.question: What is the bias-variance trade-off?
options: Fairer models are always less accurate, so pick one of the two
Simple models underfit and flexible models overfit, so balance complexity
Faster training always means fewer classes, so balance class counts
More GPU memory always means less CPU memory, so balance the two kinds of hardware
questions.explanation: Error comes partly from overly simple assumptions (bias) and partly from sensitivity to the training sample (variance). Increasing complexity lowers bias but raises variance. Regularization and validation help find the balance.

source.title: scikit-learn, Underfitting vs. Overfitting

questions.question: What does L2 regularization (weight decay) do?
options: Rescales the input features to zero mean and unit variance
Adds a penalty on squared weights, keeping weights small
Doubles the learning rate after every training epoch
Randomly removes half the neurons at each training step
questions.explanation: L2 regularization adds lambda times the sum of squared weights to the loss, which pushes weights toward small values and reduces overfitting. Dropping neurons is dropout, and input normalization is preprocessing.

source.title: Google ML Crash Course, Overfitting: L2 regularization
